title: Automatic Enrollment in Savings
text:
In the late 1990s a large American company changed one rule in its 401(k) retirement savings plan. Before, new employees had to sign up if they wanted to save. After the change, new employees were enrolled automatically, with a default of 3 percent of pay invested in a conservative money market fund, unless they chose otherwise.

The economists Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea compared workers hired just before and just after the switch. Among those hired under the old opt-in rule, fewer than 40 percent were participating at a comparable point in their tenure. Among those hired under automatic enrollment, participation was above 85 percent. The gains were largest among younger and lower-paid workers, the groups least likely to sign up on their own.

There was a catch. Most of the automatically enrolled employees stayed exactly where the default put them: at the 3 percent rate and in the money market fund, even though many of the earlier hires who had chosen for themselves saved more and invested in stocks. The default that brought people in also anchored how much and how they saved.

Madrian and Shea called their 2001 paper "The Power of Suggestion." Their findings helped persuade employers and lawmakers to adopt automatic enrollment, which was encouraged in the United States by the Pension Protection Act of 2006.
lesson: Inertia can work for you as well as against you. Set up good habits, savings and routines so they happen by default, and then check once in a while that the default still fits.
source: Madrian, B. C., and Shea, D. F. (2001). The power of suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) participation and savings behavior. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 116(4), 1149-1187.
